text.en: Ask five friends what our country is called and you may hear India, Bharat, Hindustan and more. Why does one land have so many names? The answer lies in rivers, mountains, poems, travellers and inscriptions. In this chapter we trace the names of India in the words of Indians and of foreigners, and we see how geography shaped the idea of one land.

Today India is a modern nation with defined borders, defined states and a known population. It was very different 500 years ago, 2000 years ago or even 5000 years ago, because this region, often called the Indian Subcontinent, has had many different names and shifting boundaries. We learn about its past from ancient texts, accounts of travellers and pilgrims, and inscriptions. On a physical map the natural boundaries of the Subcontinent stand out: the great mountains in the north, and the seas to the east, south and west.
The Rig Veda, India most ancient text, is several thousand years old. It names the northwest region of the Subcontinent Sapta Sindhava, which means the land of the seven rivers. The word Sindhava comes from Sindhu, which refers to the Indus River or at times to a river in general. The Mahabharata lists many regions, such as Kashmira, Kurukshetra in parts of Haryana, Vanga in parts of Bengal, Pragjyotisha roughly in Assam, Kaccha which is today Kutch, and Kerala. Together these cover the whole geography of the Subcontinent. Ancient Indian texts are difficult to date, but scholars generally agree that the Mahabharata was written from a few centuries BCE onward. It uses the terms Bharatavarsha and Jambudvipa. Bharatavarsha clearly covers the entire Subcontinent. Several kings named Bharata appear in later literature. Jambudvipa means the island of the fruit of the jamun tree, a common tree native to India also called the jambul or Malabar plum tree. It came to mean the Indian Subcontinent. Emperor Ashoka, who lived about 250 BCE, used the name Jambudvipa in one of his inscriptions for the whole of India, which then included what is today Bangladesh, Pakistan and parts of Afghanistan. A few centuries later Bharata became the usual name. The Vishnu Purana says the country north of the ocean and south of the snowy mountains is called Bharata. The snowy mountains are the Himalayas. In north India the name is written Bharat and in south India often Bharatam, and it is the name of India in most Indian languages. A poem of ancient Tamil literature, about 2000 years ago, praises a king whose name is known from Cape Kumari in the south to the great mountain in the north, between the eastern and western oceans. So different parts of the country shared a similar idea of India. The Indian Constitution, first written in English, begins with the phrase India, that is Bharat. The Hindi version says Bharat arthat India. The Constitution came into force in 1950.
The first foreigners to mention India were the Persians of ancient Iran. In the 6th century BCE a Persian emperor gained control of the region of the Indus River, once called Sindhu. In their records and inscriptions the Persians called India Hind, Hidu or Hindu, adaptations of Sindhu. In ancient Persian, Hindu was purely a geographical term and did not refer to the Hindu religion. Using the Persian sources, the ancient Greeks called the region Indoi or Indike. They dropped the initial h of Hindu because the Greek language had no such letter. The chain is Sindhu, Hindhu, Indoi or Indike. The ancient Chinese called India Yintu or Yindu, also from Sindhu through Hindhu and Indu. Another Chinese word derived from Sindhu was Tianzhu, which could also mean heavenly master, showing their respect for India as the land of the Buddha. Xuanzang, a Chinese scholar of the 7th century CE, travelled to India, visited many parts, met scholars, collected Buddhist texts and returned to China after 17 years. There he translated the manuscripts from Sanskrit into Chinese. Several other Chinese scholars also visited India. The word Hindustan was first used in a Persian inscription about 1800 years ago. Later it became the term used by most invaders of India for the Subcontinent. Eventually the name India, derived from the Sindhu or Indus River, became the English name, and Inde the French one.

prompt.en: Explain why India has many names and where each came from.

requiredIdeas.en: Indian texts used Sapta Sindhava, Jambudvipa and Bharata
Foreigners adapted Sindhu to Hind, Indoi and Yindu
Geography such as the mountains in the north and the seas shaped the definition
The Constitution says India, that is Bharat

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking Hindu in ancient Persian meant the religion
Thinking Bharat is a modern invention

points.en: India has had many names: Sapta Sindhava, Jambudvipa and Bharata in Indian texts.
Bharata, from the Vishnu Purana description of the land between the ocean and the snowy mountains, is the name in most Indian languages.
Persians, Greeks and Chinese changed Sindhu to Hind, Indoi and Yindu, which led to India.
In ancient Persian, Hindu was a geographical term, not a religion.
The Constitution begins with India, that is Bharat.
